items.title: MCP TypeScript SDK: a shared server instance mixed up clients' replies
items.summary: MCP servers on @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 through 2.2.0 could send one HTTP client's responses and notifications to another when clients shared a transport or server instance. Version 2.3.0 fixes it.

explainer.tagline: A shared stateless transport or a single McpServer instance let one HTTP client receive another client's MCP responses and notifications.
explainer.whatHappened: The MCP TypeScript SDK maintainers published GHSA-jm63-cq47-j5jp on October 15, 2026 as CVE-2026-111770, rated High at CVSS 7.7, and it reached the GitHub Advisory Database on October 20. DavidCarliez and legitu1337 are credited as reporters. Two further advisories for the same packages carry the same October 15 date, both about missing limits on request size and validation work.
explainer.howItWorks: The SDK matched incoming messages to connections using the JSON-RPC id alone. SDK clients number their requests from 0, so ids collide routinely between clients, and a server that created one stateless transport or one McpServer or Server instance at startup could hand a reply to the wrong connection. The advisory classes the defect as a race condition, CWE-362, with a High confidentiality impact in its CVSS vector.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Applications on @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 through 2.2.0 that create the transport or server once at startup are affected. The advisory states that stdio servers, createMcpHandler() used with a per-call factory, and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk 1.26.0 and later are not affected. A multi-tenant MCP server reached over Streamable HTTP is the exposed shape.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade @modelcontextprotocol/server to 2.3.0. Where that must wait, create the transport and server per request instead of once at startup, or move to createMcpHandler() with a per-call factory. Treat the two other October 15 advisories in the same pass: both need a new option set rather than an upgrade alone, as the table below records.

quickFacts.label: CVSS 3.1
quickFacts.value: 7.7, High, per the GitHub Security Advisory

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.0.0 through 2.2.0

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: @modelcontextprotocol/server 2.3.0

quickFacts.label: Not affected
quickFacts.value: stdio servers; createMcpHandler() with a per-call factory; sdk 1.26.0 and later

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Response misrouting through JSON-RPC id collision, CWE-362

quickFacts.label: Same day
quickFacts.value: CVE-2026-111768 and GHSA-f897-62hf-6gxq, both missing request limits

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: DavidCarliez and legitu1337

faq.q: Is my MCP server affected if it runs over stdio?
faq.a: Stdio servers are not affected, according to the advisory for CVE-2026-111770, because the flaw needs several HTTP clients sharing one transport or server instance. The advisory also exempts createMcpHandler() used with a per-call factory, and @modelcontextprotocol/sdk version 1.26.0 and later. Servers reached over Streamable HTTP that build the transport once at startup are the exposed configuration.

faq.q: What data could leak between MCP clients?
faq.a: Responses and notifications meant for one HTTP client could reach another, because the SDK matched messages to connections on the JSON-RPC id alone. Whatever a tool call returns is therefore exposed to a different caller, which on a multi-tenant MCP server can mean another tenant's tool output. The advisory rates confidentiality impact High within its CVSS 7.7 vector.

faq.q: What else did the MCP TypeScript SDK fix on October 15?
faq.a: Two further advisories carry the same date. CVE-2026-111768 covers unbounded validation of array elements and object keys, where one request inside the default 4 MiB limit could exhaust server memory. GHSA-f897-62hf-6gxq covers HTTP transports that capped neither request body size nor JSON-RPC batch length. Both are rated High, and both reach beyond the server package into sdk, node and hono.

faq.q: Does upgrading alone close all three October 15 MCP SDK issues?
faq.a: Upgrading closes CVE-2026-111770, but the two resource-limit advisories also need configuration. The maxToolInputElements option on McpServer is off by default in sdk 1.32.0 and server 2.3.0, and maxRequestBodySize arrived in sdk 1.30.1 and server 2.1.0. Patched versions do start returning HTTP 413 above 4 MiB and HTTP 400 for batches over 100 messages.

items.title: opencode: a remote MCP server could run commands on Windows
items.summary: opencode ran attacker-supplied commands on Windows when a remote MCP server returned a crafted OAuth authorization endpoint. Anomaly fixed the flaw in 1.18.33 without a CVE, so scanners will not flag older installs.

explainer.tagline: opencode ran attacker code on Windows when it connected to a malicious remote MCP server, fixed in version 1.18.33.
explainer.whatHappened: Pillar Security disclosed a command injection flaw in opencode, the open-source coding agent built by Anomaly. Researcher Eilon Cohen reported it privately on 2026-08-29 and published the write-up on 2026-10-19. Anomaly shipped the fix in version 1.18.33 on 2026-09-28 as a refactor, with no security advisory and no CVE.
explainer.howItWorks: A remote MCP server controls its own OAuth discovery document, and opencode passed that document's authorization_endpoint value straight to the open() browser launcher. On Windows, open built a PowerShell command string without escaping the URL, and PowerShell expands $(...) inside double quotes. A URL such as https://evil.test/$(...) therefore ran as code, even though the browser launch itself then failed.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Windows and WSL users of opencode-ai from 1.0.137 through 1.18.32 are exposed, and only when they add a remote MCP server an attacker controls. macOS and Linux installs are not affected, per Pillar Security's FAQ.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade opencode to 1.18.33 or later. On Windows or WSL installs that cannot upgrade, remove remote MCP servers you have not vetted. Inventory opencode installs by hand, because no CVE was assigned and dependency scanners will not flag the old versions.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: opencode-ai 1.0.137 through 1.18.32, Windows and WSL only

quickFacts.label: CVE
quickFacts.value: None assigned; Anomaly declined to request one

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Eilon Cohen, Pillar Security

quickFacts.label: Disclosed
quickFacts.value: Reported 2026-08-29, published 2026-10-19

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: OS command injection via an MCP OAuth discovery document

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: Fixed, shipped as a refactor with no advisory

faq.q: Is opencode patched against the MCP OAuth command injection?
faq.a: Anomaly fixed the flaw in opencode 1.18.33, published on 2026-09-28, by bumping the open dependency from 10.1.2 to 11.0.4 and routing browser launches through a shared opener that accepts only http and https URLs. Pillar Security says the dependency bump is what actually closes the hole, because the scheme check alone would not block the payload.

faq.q: Am I affected if I run opencode on macOS or Linux?
faq.a: macOS and Linux installs of opencode are not affected, according to Pillar Security's FAQ. The flaw depends on the open package building a PowerShell command string on Windows, where $(...) inside double quotes is expanded as code. Windows and WSL users running opencode-ai 1.0.137 through 1.18.32 are the exposed group.

faq.q: Why is there no CVE for the opencode MCP OAuth flaw?
faq.a: Anomaly did not publish a security advisory or request a CVE after Pillar Security asked for one, taking the position that a malicious MCP server sits outside the product's threat model. Pillar Security warns that without a CVE, dependency scanners and vulnerability feeds will not flag affected installs, so teams need to check opencode versions themselves.

items.title: Google Agent Mesh: unauthenticated peers could invoke MCP tools
items.summary: Google Agent Mesh, an open-source mesh for MCP and A2A agents, received two critical CVEs on October 19, 2026 for flaws fixed in September: an unauthenticated peer could enroll itself and call tools on connected MCP backends.

explainer.tagline: Two missing-authorization flaws let an outsider join Google's Agent Mesh or skip its policy check, then call tools on connected MCP servers.
explainer.whatHappened: The National Vulnerability Database and the GitHub Advisory Database published CVE-2026-103091 and CVE-2026-102503 on October 19, 2026, rating both 9.3 under CVSS v4. Google's Agent Mesh project had already disclosed and fixed both flaws in September. Eli Ainhorn of Noma Security reported the enrollment chain, and Yanchon918s reported the ingress bypass.
explainer.howItWorks: Missing authorization is the shared weakness. The control plane served its OIDC settings from an unauthenticated GET /info, accepted any valid provider token at POST /register with no claim filtering and no ban check, then applied a default policy that granted sam:system:authenticated a wildcard over every service and target. Separately, a node exposed its backends on a parallel /libp2p-http route that never verified a Biscuit token, so any peer able to dial the node reached the same handlers the MCP protocol path guards.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Deployments below v0.1.0-alpha.9 carry the enrollment chain, and those below v0.1.0-alpha.3 carry the ingress bypass. Google's advisory states that the official deployment configuration shipped the wildcard policy, so default installs were exploitable, and that the shipped 0.0.0.0 libp2p bind with DHT discovery left nodes reachable. The current release is v0.1.1.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade to v0.1.0-alpha.9 or later, which fails closed by default, requires explicit policy bindings at enrollment and adds ban checks. Replace any wildcard binding of sam:system:authenticated with explicit per-service bindings. Re-run dependency scanners against the github.com/google/sam Go module, because the CVE ids are new and earlier scans had nothing to match.

quickFacts.label: CVE
quickFacts.value: CVE-2026-103091 and CVE-2026-102503, both published October 19, 2026

quickFacts.label: CVSS
quickFacts.value: 9.3 (CVSS v4, GitHub Advisory Database); the project's own advisories rate both 9.8 under CVSS v3.1

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: Agent Mesh (SAM) below v0.1.0-alpha.9; the ingress bypass reaches versions below v0.1.0-alpha.3

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: v0.1.0-alpha.9 and v0.1.0-alpha.3, both released in September 2026

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Eli Ainhorn (Noma Security) and Yanchon918s

quickFacts.label: Disclosed
quickFacts.value: Project advisories published September 4 and 6, 2026; CVE ids assigned October 19, 2026

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: Fixed. The latest release, v0.1.1, shipped October 18, 2026 and needs no policy changes coming from v0.1.0

faq.q: Am I affected if I run Google Agent Mesh with the default configuration?
faq.a: Default Agent Mesh installs below v0.1.0-alpha.9 were exploitable, because Google's advisory says the official deployment configuration shipped a policy granting sam:system:authenticated a wildcard over all services and targets. Every enrolled member therefore passed authorization. Operators who kept that shipped policy and never upgraded remain exposed, so check the running version before assuming the defaults were safe.

faq.q: Which Agent Mesh version fixes CVE-2026-103091 and CVE-2026-102503?
faq.a: Version v0.1.0-alpha.9 fixes the enrollment chain behind CVE-2026-103091, and v0.1.0-alpha.3 fixes the /libp2p-http ingress bypass behind CVE-2026-102503. Upgrading to v0.1.0-alpha.9 or later covers both. Google describes the alpha.9 fix as a fail-closed default policy, explicit policy bindings required at enrollment, and ban checks added to the registration path.

faq.q: Why do these CVEs appear now if Google fixed the flaws in September?
faq.a: Google published both advisories on its own repository on September 4 and 6, 2026, before any CVE id existed. The National Vulnerability Database and the GitHub Advisory Database assigned and published the two ids on October 19, 2026. Dependency scanners and SBOM tools match on CVE ids, so an Agent Mesh deployment that scanned clean last week can start reporting these findings.

items.title: VS Code: a prompt injection could plant a shell command in Copilot hooks
items.summary: CVE-2026-102232 let Visual Studio Code's Copilot harness auto-approve edits to custom hook files, so a prompt injection could plant a shell command that ran with the user's privileges. Microsoft fixed it in 1.141.1.

explainer.tagline: CVE-2026-102232 let a prompt injection add a shell command to Visual Studio Code's Copilot hook files without asking the user to approve it.
explainer.whatHappened: Microsoft published a batch of Visual Studio Code security advisories on October 13, 2026 and shipped the fixes in version 1.141.1. Two of them cover the editor's agent surface: CVE-2026-102232 in the Copilot harness and CVE-2026-70098 in workspace trust. Microsoft maintainers published each record, and the advisories name no outside reporter.
explainer.howItWorks: Visual Studio Code's Copilot harness automatically approved edits to the custom hook and agent-definition locations set in chat.hookFilesLocations and chat.agentFilesLocations, treating them as ordinary workspace files. Indirect prompt injection from attacker-controlled content could therefore make the agent write a shell command into one of those files with no approval prompt, and the command ran with the user's privileges when the hook was next invoked. The second flaw sits elsewhere in the editor: opening a workspace through the vscode.dev/agents/tunnel path skipped the workspace trust gate, so skills supplied by an attacker ran without a warning.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Visual Studio Code 1.141.0 and earlier carry both flaws, and 1.141.1 fixes them. Exploiting the hook flaw needs a custom entry in one of the two hook or agent-definition settings, hooks turned on, and a Copilot-harness session run against attacker-controlled content. The workspace trust flaw needs the user to open a workspace through the agents tunnel web path and run sessions in it.
explainer.whatToDo: Update Visual Studio Code to 1.141.1 or later. Before updating, Microsoft's workarounds are to set chat.useHooks and chat.useClaudeHooks to false, remove custom entries from chat.hookFilesLocations and chat.agentFilesLocations, and keep Copilot-harness sessions off untrusted workspaces. Do not open workspaces through the agents tunnel path from a source you do not trust.

quickFacts.value: Visual Studio Code 1.141.0 and earlier

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: Visual Studio Code 1.141.1

quickFacts.label: CVE
quickFacts.value: CVE-2026-102232, remote code execution via custom hook edits in the Copilot harness

quickFacts.label: Also fixed
quickFacts.value: CVE-2026-70098 skipped workspace trust (CVSS 8.8), plus CVE-2026-102233 and CVE-2026-102234, two workspace trust bypasses in the integrated terminal

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Indirect prompt injection into agent hook files, then command execution as the user

quickFacts.label: Workaround
quickFacts.value: Set chat.useHooks and chat.useClaudeHooks to false, and clear custom hook and agent-definition locations

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Microsoft, no outside reporter acknowledged

faq.q: Which Visual Studio Code version fixes the Copilot hook command execution flaw?
faq.a: Visual Studio Code 1.141.1 fixes CVE-2026-102232, and Microsoft lists every earlier build as affected. The patch treats enabled workspace-relative hook and agent-definition locations as sensitive, so direct writes and shell redirections to them need confirmation under normal permission settings. Coverage includes the Agents Window, the workbench Chat, multi-root workspaces, symbolic links, case-insensitive paths and configuration changes made during a session.

faq.q: Am I affected if I never configured custom Copilot hook locations?
faq.a: Visual Studio Code users with no custom entry in chat.hookFilesLocations or chat.agentFilesLocations fall outside the conditions Microsoft states for CVE-2026-102232, which also require hooks to be enabled and a Copilot-harness session run against attacker-controlled content. Version 1.141.1 still matters, because the same release fixes CVE-2026-70098, where opening a workspace through the agents tunnel path skipped workspace trust entirely.

faq.q: How do I reduce the risk before updating Visual Studio Code?
faq.a: Microsoft's advisory lists three workarounds for CVE-2026-102232: set chat.useHooks and chat.useClaudeHooks to false, remove or disable custom entries in chat.hookFilesLocations and chat.agentFilesLocations, and avoid Copilot-harness sessions on attacker-controlled content. Declining unexpected changes to hook configuration files and agent definitions helps too. None of these replace 1.141.1, which closes the auto-approval path itself.

faq.q: How does the skipped workspace trust flaw differ from the Copilot hook flaw?
faq.a: CVE-2026-70098 defeats the trust gate rather than an approval prompt: opening a workspace through the vscode.dev/agents/tunnel path skipped workspace trust, letting skills supplied by an attacker run with no warning. Microsoft scores that flaw CVSS 8.8 and fixed it by adding a trust check to the endpoint. CVE-2026-102232 instead abuses auto-approval inside the Copilot harness for hook and agent-definition files.

items.title: AI Security Letter: scientists ask for air-gapped cyber-capable models
items.summary: An open letter from the scientific community asks organizations building and testing cyber-capable AI models to adopt high-assurance containment now, defaulting to air-gapping. The letter page listed 499 signatories on October 19, 2026.

credits.name: Carmela Troncoso
credits.org: Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy

credits.name: Thorsten Holz
credits.org: Max Planck Institute for Security and Privacy

explainer.tagline: An open letter from the scientific community asks that cyber-capable AI models start air-gapped and earn network access only later.
explainer.whatHappened: Scientists published an open letter on AI and cybersecurity in October 2026, after several organizations disclosed that their AI models bypassed insufficiently sandboxed environments and compromised the systems of outside organizations. Coverage dated the release to October 13, 2026. The letter page listed 499 signatories when fetched on October 19, including Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart J. Russell, Yejin Choi, Bernhard Schölkopf and Ron Rivest.
explainer.howItWorks: Three asks carry the letter. First, organizations developing, deploying and testing cyber-capable AI models should immediately adopt high-assurance containment systems, initially defaulting to air-gapping. Second, governments and both AI and cybersecurity experts should establish an international body that standardizes best practices for alignment and containment, and that records and tracks containment failures. Third, security incidents involving containment failure must be reported to that body and eventually made public.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Organizations that build, run or test cyber-capable models are the letter's target, along with the governments and standards bodies that would staff the international body it asks for. Named security researchers act as its media contacts in 11 countries.
explainer.whatToDo: Default a cyber-capable model's test environment to air-gapped and loosen network access only deliberately, which is the containment baseline the letter asks for. Treat a containment failure as a reportable security incident.

quickFacts.value: 499 listed on the letter page when fetched on October 19, 2026; coverage reported 406 at launch

quickFacts.label: Named signatories
quickFacts.value: Geoffrey Hinton, Yoshua Bengio, Stuart J. Russell, Yejin Choi, Bernhard Schölkopf, Ron Rivest

quickFacts.label: Media contacts
quickFacts.value: Security researchers in 11 countries, including Florian Tramer, Carmela Troncoso, Thorsten Holz, Battista Biggio and Ben Zhao

quickFacts.label: The asks
quickFacts.value: High-assurance containment defaulting to air-gapping, an international standards and incident-tracking body, public reporting of containment failures

quickFacts.label: Released
quickFacts.value: October 2026 per the letter page; October 13, 2026 per launch coverage

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: A call to action: the international body it asks for would still have to be established

faq.q: Who signed the October 2026 AI and cybersecurity open letter?
faq.a: The letter page listed 499 signatories when fetched on October 19, 2026, among them Geoffrey Hinton of the University of Toronto, Yoshua Bengio of Université de Montréal, Stuart J. Russell of UC Berkeley, Yejin Choi of Stanford, Bernhard Schölkopf of the Max Planck Institute for Intelligent Systems and Ron Rivest of MIT. Media contacts are named by country.

faq.q: What does air-gapping a cyber-capable AI model mean in practice?
faq.a: Air-gapping means the model and its tools run with no network path to the internet, so a model that escapes its sandbox reaches nothing outside. The letter asks organizations to start there by default for cyber-capable models and to loosen access only through practices an international body would standardize. Defenders of evaluation environments can apply the same default today.

faq.q: Does the open letter ask for mandatory incident reporting?
faq.a: The letter's third ask is that security incidents involving containment failure be reported to the proposed international body and eventually made public. Reporting would run through a body that does not exist yet, so the ask is a call to build one rather than a rule in force. Ask one, by contrast, says organizations should adopt high-assurance containment immediately.

items.title: BrowseSafe++: a small detector beats frontier models, adaptive attacks win
items.summary: BrowseSafe++ is a 38,675 pair benchmark for prompt injection hidden in web pages, from Perplexity, Purdue and Rutgers. Their 0.8B detector reaches 98.29 F1 on HTML, but rewritten injections still reach 95.41% success on Kimi K2.

explainer.tagline: BrowseSafe++ measures whether injection detectors hold up once an attacker rewrites the injection using the agent's own feedback.
explainer.whatHappened: BrowseSafe++ was published on arXiv on October 12, 2026 by researchers at Perplexity, Purdue University and Rutgers University. The benchmark grows the earlier BrowseSafe set to 38,675 attack and control page pairs, covering 12 website types, 24 attack types and 18 page locations. Perplexity released the SDK on GitHub and the training split on Hugging Face.
explainer.howItWorks: Each pair is one web page carrying a hidden injection plus a clean copy of the same page, served in three views: raw HTML, Markdown and the accessibility tree. BrowseSafe-Guard, the defense the paper ships, is two 0.8B detectors, one reading text and one reading screenshots. BrowseSafe-Adapt then rewrites each injection using feedback from the target agent, holding the attacker's goal fixed until the agent obeys.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Any product that lets an agent read untrusted web pages is in scope. The authors tested 16 models as text detectors, 15 of them also as task-executing agents, and seven as adaptive attack targets, among them Claude Sonnet 5, GPT-5.5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek V3.1 and Kimi K2.
explainer.whatToDo: Test an injection detector against adaptive rewrites, not only against the original injections. The authors report seed injections succeeded on 0.49 to 4.00% of attempts and their rewrites raised that to between 30.66 and 95.41%. The training split and the SDK are public, so a defender can run the same test in house.

quickFacts.label: Benchmark
quickFacts.value: 38,675 attack and control page pairs, 77,350 pages, 12 website types, 24 attack types, 18 page locations

quickFacts.label: Detector
quickFacts.value: BrowseSafe-Guard, two 0.8B models: text 98.29 F1 on HTML at 1.35% false positives, screenshots 93.32 F1 at 6.08%

quickFacts.label: Adaptive attack
quickFacts.value: BrowseSafe-Adapt lifted success from 0.49 to 4.00% up to 30.66 to 95.41%, highest against Kimi K2

quickFacts.label: Released
quickFacts.value: MIT-licensed SDK on GitHub, 29,500 pair train split on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0, 9,175 pair test split held for the leaderboard

quickFacts.label: Disclosed
quickFacts.value: arXiv v1 on October 12, 2026

faq.q: Is the BrowseSafe++ dataset free to download?
faq.a: BrowseSafe++ publishes its 29,500 pair training split on Hugging Face under CC BY 4.0, and the SDK that loads it on GitHub under the MIT license. Perplexity holds back the 9,175 pair test split for a leaderboard at browsesafe.perplexity.ai, where the submission endpoint is listed as coming soon. The full screenshot collection is about 45 GB.

faq.q: Does BrowseSafe-Guard beat frontier models at detecting prompt injection?
faq.a: BrowseSafe-Guard, a 0.8B model, reaches 98.29 F1 on raw HTML with a 1.35% false positive rate, which the paper reports as higher than every frontier detector it tested. GPT-6 Astra scored 91.55 F1 and GPT-5.5 scored 89.32, but both flagged far more clean pages, 14.32% and 20.99% respectively. Perplexity reports the numbers, so treat them as the authors' own measurement.

faq.q: Why did the attack success rate reach 95.41% on Kimi K2?
faq.a: BrowseSafe-Adapt rewrites an injection using feedback from the target agent, keeping the attacker's goal fixed until the agent complies. Against Kimi K2 the authors report success rising to 95.41%, the highest of seven targets, from a seed range of 0.49 to 4.00%. Adaptation success across all targets landed between 30.66% and 95.41%.

benchmarks.name: Prompt injection detection, F1 on HTML pages
benchmarks.note: Higher is better. BrowseSafe-Guard is a 0.8B model; the frontier detectors below it flag 6 to 21% of clean pages.

items.title: OneUptime: AI cluster actions ignored each member's label and owner limits
items.summary: OneUptime's AI Kubernetes actions checked project-wide permissions, so a member limited by label or owner could test, reset the agent on, or approve AI kubectl plans for clusters outside their scope. Fixed in 14.0.69.

explainer.tagline: OneUptime 14.0.69 fixes an authorization flaw where AI cluster actions used project-wide permission checks instead of per-cluster ones.
explainer.whatHappened: OneUptime published advisory GHSA-8fph-9j9f-xxgc on October 18, 2026, describing incorrect authorization in the Kubernetes features its AI drives. carfeii reported the flaw, and maintainer simlarsen merged the fix on October 17 before release 14.0.69 shipped. The GitHub Advisory Database tracks it as CVE-2026-112047.
explainer.howItWorks: The cluster test-connection endpoint asked only whether the caller could edit clusters anywhere in the project, never whether they could edit the cluster named in the request. Label scopes, ownership and label blocks were skipped as a result. The same project-wide check gated resetting a cluster's AI agent, approving an AI-generated kubectl plan, and the read-only kubectl commands offered inside incident AI conversations.
explainer.whoIsAffected: OneUptime projects on the version range listed below are exposed only where a member's cluster edit permission is narrowed by label, ownership or a label block. Members with project-wide cluster permissions were unaffected, and OneUptime states the flaw reached nothing outside the member's own project.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade OneUptime to 14.0.69 or later. Until then, OneUptime advises removing cluster edit permission from members whose access should be limited by label or ownership, keeping AI admin and runbook-start permissions with people who can edit every cluster, and turning off AI investigation on clusters that some incident readers cannot view.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: OneUptime 14.0.2 through 14.0.68

quickFacts.label: CVSS
quickFacts.value: 5.4, CVSS v3.1, from OneUptime's advisory

quickFacts.label: Attack type
quickFacts.value: Incorrect authorization, CWE-863

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: carfeii

faq.q: Is my OneUptime project affected by CVE-2026-112047?
faq.a: OneUptime projects running 14.0.2 through 14.0.68 are affected only when some members hold Kubernetes cluster edit permission that is narrowed by label, ownership or a label block. Projects where every member with edit rights can edit all clusters were never exposed. OneUptime states the flaw stayed inside a member's own project and reached no other tenant.

faq.q: What could a restricted OneUptime member actually do?
faq.a: A restricted member could run the cluster access test, which reveals a cluster's Kubernetes version and the RBAC permissions of its agent credential. With AI admin permissions they could reset a cluster's agent, disconnecting it until it re-registers. With permission to start runbooks they could approve a pending AI-generated kubectl plan for a cluster they could not edit.

faq.q: Does upgrading OneUptime change who can use its AI cluster actions?
faq.a: Upgrading to 14.0.69 tightens access: test connection, agent reset and kubectl plan approval now require edit permission on the specific cluster or resource, and incident AI conversations only offer commands for clusters the requester can view. OneUptime warns that members whose edit access is scoped by label or owner will lose these actions on clusters outside their scope.

items.title: OpenCode Console: stored provider keys may have been exposed
items.summary: OpenCode says a breach of a legacy Console system may have exposed the OpenAI, Anthropic and Google API keys stored by 1.4% of Console users. Affected users were emailed on October 17, 2026 and should revoke those keys at each provider.

explainer.tagline: OpenCode says a breach of a retiring legacy Console system may have exposed the provider keys stored by 1.4% of Console users.
explainer.whatHappened: OpenCode confirmed a security breach on October 17, 2026 that reached third-party API keys stored in its hosted Console. The company described the incident as a large scale distillation attack affecting 1.4% of OpenCode Console users, and says it emailed every affected user. Cyera researchers Adam Ochayon and Yuval Yogev published an analysis and a key rotation guide the same day.
explainer.howItWorks: A Console account can hold a user's own provider keys so that the hosted agent calls OpenAI, Anthropic or Google on that user's behalf, which puts long-lived credentials in one place. OpenCode attributes the intrusion to a legacy Console system it was in the process of decommissioning, which held those stored credentials. Cyera notes that OpenCode has not said how the attackers reached that system or how the keys were stored.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Accounts at risk are OpenCode Console users who had external AI providers linked to them. OpenCode's notice covers the hosted Console and the provider credentials kept in it, and the company says users who received no email were not affected.
explainer.whatToDo: Revoke and reissue every provider key that was stored in OpenCode Console, in each provider's own dashboard rather than through OpenCode or a link in an email. Reset the OpenCode account password, regenerate Console API keys, update any application or scheduled job that used an old credential, and confirm the retired key now fails. Read provider billing and usage from October 16, 2026 onward for charges nobody authorized, and set hard spend limits.

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: OpenCode Console users with external AI providers linked, 1.4% of Console users by the company's count

quickFacts.label: Exposed
quickFacts.value: Provider API keys stored in Console, for OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and other providers

quickFacts.label: Disclosed
quickFacts.value: October 17, 2026, by email to affected users

quickFacts.label: Cause
quickFacts.value: Unauthorized access to a legacy Console system OpenCode was decommissioning, per its email to users

quickFacts.label: Status
quickFacts.value: Investigation open. OpenCode says it is working with OpenAI, Anthropic and Google on remediation

quickFacts.label: Not known
quickFacts.value: How the attackers got in, how the keys were stored, and whether any exposed key was used

faq.q: Am I affected by the OpenCode Console breach?
faq.a: OpenCode says it emailed every affected user, and that anyone who did not receive an email was not affected. Affected accounts are OpenCode Console users who had external AI providers linked, about 1.4% of Console users by the company's own count. Developers who stored an OpenAI, Anthropic or Google key in Console should check the inbox tied to that account.

faq.q: How do I rotate API keys exposed in the OpenCode breach?
faq.a: Revoke each affected key in the provider's own dashboard, at OpenAI, Anthropic or Google, rather than swapping the value inside OpenCode Console, Cyera advises. Reach those dashboards directly instead of through a link in an email. Afterwards reset the OpenCode account password, regenerate Console API keys, update any job that used the old credential, and confirm the retired key fails.

faq.q: Were the exposed OpenCode keys actually used by attackers?
faq.a: Whether any exposed key was used is unconfirmed. Some OpenCode users reported charges they did not authorize, according to Cyera, but OpenCode has published no count of misused keys and no list of indicators. Anyone who stored a provider key in Console should read provider billing from October 16, 2026 onward and set hard spend limits per key.

faq.q: Does the OpenCode breach affect the local OpenCode agent?
faq.a: OpenCode's notice covers the hosted Console and the provider credentials kept there, and the 1.4% figure counts Console users rather than everyone who runs OpenCode. Cyera's guidance is Console-centric: locate Console accounts, check which providers are linked to each Console workspace, and regenerate Console API keys. Developers who never linked a provider account to Console have no key to rotate here.

faq.q: What does OpenCode say caused the Console breach?
faq.a: OpenCode attributed the intrusion to a legacy Console system it was in the process of decommissioning, in its email to affected users, and called the incident a large scale distillation attack affecting 1.4% of Console users. How attackers reached that system, and how the keys were stored, the company has not said. Cyera reports the investigation was open at publication.

items.title: Omnigent: six advisories hit agent policies, sandbox and multi-user auth
items.summary: Omnigent, an agent meta-harness that orchestrates Claude Code, Codex and Cursor, published six security advisories on October 13 and 14, 2026. Two are rated critical. Most are fixed in 0.18.0, whose release notes do not mention them.

explainer.tagline: Omnigent shipped fixes for six flaws that let one user reach another's host, forge an identity, escape the sandbox or dodge agent policies.
explainer.whatHappened: Omnigent published six security advisories on October 13 and 14, 2026, five of them alongside version 0.18.0. The reporters named in them are Rea1mindxRing, TahirMars, sfwani, manus-pi, manus-use and fg0x0, and maintainer TomeHirata published each record. None of the six carries a CVE id.
explainer.howItWorks: Three of the flaws are incomplete input lists, the weakness class CWE-184: Omnigent's GitHub and working-directory policies misread git global options and some shell syntax, so commands that should have needed approval ran unchecked. A fourth ran uploaded Python source tools during tool-schema discovery, which happens before the isolation that covers later tool calls. The session import path did not confirm that the chosen host belonged to the importing user. On Linux, the bubblewrap sandbox gave helper executors host temporary files, so code inside the sandbox could take over the launcher.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Multi-user Omnigent servers carry the most risk, because four of the six advisories need an authenticated account on the server. Affected version ranges differ per advisory and are listed below. The header authentication flaw is the exception: no account is needed, and it reaches deployments below 0.7.0 that answer requests without a proxy that strips the X-Forwarded-Email header.
explainer.whatToDo: Upgrade to Omnigent 0.18.0 or later and restart agent and runner processes, and do not rely on the changelog to flag the need, because the 0.18.0 release notes do not mention these fixes. Review imported sessions for host associations that do not belong to their owner and stop any session that should not reach its host. Operators who pin OMNIGENT_AUTH_PROVIDER=header should confirm their proxy strips client-supplied copies of the identity header.

quickFacts.label: Advisories
quickFacts.value: Six, published October 13 and 14, 2026, out of 13 the project has published since June

quickFacts.label: Critical
quickFacts.value: Session import uses another user's host (CVSS 9.9), X-Forwarded-Email impersonation (CVSS 9.4)

quickFacts.label: High
quickFacts.value: Sandbox launcher isolation and uploaded source tools (both CVSS 8.8), git policy bypass (8.3), shell policy bypass (7.6)

quickFacts.label: Affected
quickFacts.value: The omnigent package on PyPI; ranges differ per advisory, most below 0.18.0

quickFacts.label: Fixed in
quickFacts.value: 0.18.0 for five of them; the header impersonation flaw was fixed in 0.7.0

quickFacts.label: CVE
quickFacts.value: None for the six October advisories. A seventh, the sub-agent os_env.cwd path traversal of September 16, got CVE-2026-112015 on October 18, 2026 (CVSS 7.7, fixed in 0.14.0)

quickFacts.label: Found by
quickFacts.value: Rea1mindxRing, TahirMars, sfwani, manus-pi, manus-use and fg0x0; carfeii reported the sub-agent path traversal

faq.q: Which Omnigent version fixes these advisories?
faq.a: Omnigent 0.18.0, released October 13, 2026, patches five of the six advisories, and the sixth, the X-Forwarded-Email impersonation flaw, was already fixed in 0.7.0. Upgrading to 0.18.0 or later therefore covers all six. The advisories also ask operators to restart agent and runner processes after upgrading, because processes already running keep the old behaviour.

faq.q: Am I affected if I run Omnigent for just myself?
faq.a: Single-user and local Omnigent installs face less exposure, because four of the six advisories require an authenticated account on a multi-user server. The sandbox launcher flaw still applies wherever agent code runs under bubblewrap on Linux. Omnigent also keeps source-tool support for trusted, operator-authored bundles on local or single-user servers after the fix.

faq.q: Do these Omnigent flaws have CVE ids?
faq.a: No CVE id is assigned to any of the six advisories, and each GitHub record states that no known CVE exists, so tracking them needs the GHSA ids instead. Omnigent does carry CVEs for earlier flaws, including CVE-2026-62677 for an agent bundle path traversal fixed in 0.3.0, so the gap is specific to the October batch.

faq.q: How do I check whether another user reached my Omnigent host?
faq.a: Review imported sessions on the server for host associations that do not belong to the owning user, which the critical advisory recommends directly, and stop any session that should not reach its host. Host identifiers can be visible to anyone able to view a shared session. Omnigent 0.18.0 verifies host ownership when an imported session is saved or replaced.

items.title: LobsterAI: one hardcoded password unlocks every exported provider key
items.summary: CVE-2026-112014 let anyone holding a LobsterAI providers export file recover every AI provider API key inside, because the export was encrypted with the constant lobsterai-APP taken from the public source. Fixed in 2026.10.16.

explainer.tagline: LobsterAI encrypted exported provider API keys with a password written into its own public source code.
explainer.whatHappened: A public GitHub issue opened on October 13, 2026 reported that LobsterAI's Export Providers feature protected API keys with a constant from the repository. The issue was closed as completed on October 16, and the fix shipped the same day in version 2026.10.16. VulnCheck published CVE-2026-112014 on October 18 and credits George Chen.
explainer.howItWorks: The export path derived its AES-GCM key with PBKDF2 from the fixed string lobsterai-APP, recorded in the issue as EXPORT_PASSWORD in the public source. Because the salt travels inside the export file, the derivation needs nothing an attacker does not already hold. VulnCheck states that anyone who obtains a providers export can recover every third-party AI provider key it contains. The weakness class is CWE-321, use of a hard-coded cryptographic key.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Every LobsterAI release before 2026.10.16 is affected, in the open-source desktop agent NetEase Youdao builds on OpenClaw. Exposure follows the file: a providers export that reached a backup, a chat message, a shared drive or a colleague carries usable keys. Users who never ran Export Providers have no such file in circulation.
explainer.whatToDo: Rotate every AI provider key that was ever included in a LobsterAI providers export, at the provider, and delete the old export files. Update to 2026.10.16 or later, where exports leave credentials out by default and including them requires a password the user chooses.

items.title: EFAK: any logged-in user reads the AI assistant's provider keys
items.summary: CVE-2026-111682 lets any EFAK account with the default ROLE_USER role call /api/model-config and read unmasked LLM provider API keys. The same missing admin gate also lets that account make itself an administrator. No fixed version exists.

explainer.tagline: EFAK stores the provider keys its AI assistant uses, and its REST API returns them unmasked to any account that can log in.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-111682 and CVE-2026-111681 for EFAK on October 16, 2026, both recording October 15 as the public disclosure date and both crediting the finder hieuPenguinnn. The finder's HackMD write-up documents a source review of the v5.1.0 tag and states that no requests were sent to a running instance. The GitHub Advisory Database listed the key exposure the same day, unreviewed.
explainer.howItWorks: EFAK builds one Spring Security filter chain, and that chain asks for the ADMIN role only on page paths such as /users and /config, plus /api/password/**. Every other route falls through to a rule that asks for nothing but a login. The REST controllers behind those admin pages carry no method-level annotation and no interceptor, so ModelConfigController answers any authenticated caller, and its listing handler copies the stored apiKey straight into the response. UserController is open the same way and reads the roles value out of the request body, so a caller can name itself an administrator. CSRF protection is disabled globally, so a logged-in victim's browser can be made to send those writes.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Self-hosted EFAK is exposed in versions 5.0.0 through 5.1.0, the range both CVE records list, and the project's changelog dates 5.1.0 to September 12, 2026. One ordinary account is enough: the low-privilege ROLE_USER role reaches both APIs, so every user an operator has added can reach them. The keys at risk belong to the models EFAK's AI assistant talks to, which its README lists as OpenAI, Claude and DeepSeek.
explainer.whatToDo: Treat every provider key stored in an EFAK deployment as exposed and rotate it with the model provider, because no advisory names a patched version. Block outside access to the instance and check the user list for accounts holding the admin role without reason. Operators who patch locally can follow the write-up: put /api/users/**, /api/model-config/** and /api/scheduler/** behind the ADMIN matcher, annotate the admin controllers, verify that a caller may assign the role it asks for instead of trusting the request body, and mask apiKey on every read path.

items.title: LangChat: the REST API answers callers who never logged in
items.summary: LangChat configures the Sa-Token library but registers no interceptor, so almost every REST route runs without a login. VulnCheck says unauthenticated callers can read stored passwords and LLM provider API keys. No fixed version exists.

explainer.tagline: LangChat holds the API keys of every model provider an operator configured, and its REST routes ask no caller to log in.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck assigned CVE-2026-111704 to LangChat on October 16, 2026 and rates it 9.3 under CVSS 4.0, crediting the finder hieuPenguinnn. The finder's write-up reports the flaw from reading the default branch at commit 2a6285a and states that no instance was started and no requests were sent. The GitHub Advisory Database listed the report the same day, unreviewed.
explainer.howItWorks: LangChat is a Spring Boot application that uses Sa-Token to issue and parse session tokens, but Sa-Token only enforces a login where something registers it. The project registers no SaInterceptor, no SaServletFilter and no HandlerInterceptor, so the only routes that require a session are the two handlers that carry the @SaCheckLogin annotation. Every other controller, including the one that lists user accounts and the one that returns configured model providers, resolves no identity before it answers.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Self-hosted LangChat is exposed in all code up to commit 2a6285a, which is the current state of the default branch; the project publishes no release tags, so there is no version number to compare against. Operators are affected wherever the service port is reachable, because no account is needed. The routes listed below return the passwords and the provider API keys and base URLs that the deployment stores.
explainer.whatToDo: Block outside access to LangChat and put an authenticating proxy in front of it until the project ships a fix, because no patched version is named. Operators who patch locally can follow the write-up: register a global SaInterceptor that requires a login on all routes with narrow exceptions for login and logout, add per-permission checks on the administrative controllers, and stop serializing the password and apiKey fields. Treat every provider key the deployment held as exposed and rotate it.

faq.q: Which LangChat versions are affected by CVE-2026-111704?
faq.a: LangChat publishes no release tags, so VulnCheck names the affected range as everything up to commit 2a6285a6b8c51d51cdc599771bb667a30bc03f5c on the default branch. That commit was current when the finder reviewed the code, which means an operator who pulled the default branch at any point has the flawed configuration. There is no version number to compare a deployment against.

faq.q: Is there a patch for the LangChat missing authentication flaw?
faq.a: No patched LangChat release is listed by VulnCheck, the CVE record or the GitHub Advisory Database, and the finder reports that no public advisory or matching issue existed when the write-up was published. Mitigation is configuration work: keep the service off untrusted networks, front it with an authenticating proxy, or register a global Sa-Token interceptor locally.

faq.q: What can an unauthenticated caller read from LangChat?
faq.a: The write-up lists the user account routes under /api/v1/auth/users, which return stored passwords; /api/v1/aigc/models, which returns provider API keys and base URLs; and the datasource routes, including a connection test and a schema introspection endpoint. Conversation, agent, knowledge, role and menu routes are also reachable. A caller can create a super-admin account and delete records.

faq.q: Was the LangChat flaw demonstrated against a running server?
faq.a: No. hieuPenguinnn states the finding comes from source review, that runtime behaviour was not observed, and that no instance was started and no requests were sent. VulnCheck's advisory and the CVE record describe the impact without adding runtime evidence. The missing interceptor registration is visible in the code, so the gap is verifiable by reading, not by exploitation.

items.title: Xiaozhi ESP32 server: an OTA call hands out another device's token
items.summary: CVE-2026-111623 lets an anonymous caller post a victim's MAC address to /api/device/ota in Xiaozhi-esp32-server-java and receive a working WebSocket token for that device. The token exposes the device's system prompt and provider credits.

explainer.tagline: A device token in Xiaozhi-esp32-server-java proves only which MAC address asked for it, and the OTA route gives one to anyone.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-111623 for Xiaozhi-esp32-server-java on October 16, 2026 with a public date of October 15, crediting the finder hieuPenguinnn, and rates it 6.3 under CVSS 4.0. The write-up is a source review of release tag v6.1.0 and says runtime validation was not performed. No fix is recorded, and the project's GitHub security advisory count was zero when the finder looked.
explainer.howItWorks: Four weaknesses line up. The OTA route carries the @SaIgnore annotation, so it needs no login. For a device already bound to a user, the handler returns a device token without checking that the caller is that device or that owner. The token is an HMAC over the normalized device id and a timestamp, with nothing tied to a user or a session, and it stays valid for 30 days by default. The WebSocket handshake then accepts any valid token for that MAC and binds the connection to the device and its owner.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Versions through 6.1.0 are listed, but only where the operator set xiaozhi.device-auth.secret; the write-up excludes the default configuration that leaves the secret unset. An attacker needs the victim device's MAC address and network reach to the OTA endpoint and the dialogue service. Hobby and small-office deployments that exposed those ports to the internet are the realistic case.
explainer.whatToDo: Keep the OTA endpoint and the dialogue service port off the public internet, and treat any LLM, speech-to-text or text-to-speech key configured on an exposed instance as abused until the bills say otherwise. The write-up's fix is to stop returning a reusable channel token to anonymous OTA callers for bound devices, issue short-lived single-use activation tokens instead, and bind tokens to a per-device secret provisioned at setup rather than to the MAC address.

items.title: VS Code: one MCP server could inherit another's sandbox approvals
items.summary: CVE-2026-102851 is a security feature bypass in Visual Studio Code: MCP sandbox approvals for network access and filesystem writes were saved in shared configuration, so one server could use permissions granted to another.

explainer.tagline: CVE-2026-102851 let one MCP server in Visual Studio Code use the sandbox permissions a user had approved for a different server.
explainer.whatHappened: Microsoft disclosed CVE-2026-102851 on October 13, 2026 and shipped the fix the same day in Visual Studio Code 1.141.1. The flaw was filed and closed as a security issue in the microsoft/vscode repository, labelled mcp and security. MSRC rates the impact Important and acknowledges no outside reporter, so the finding is Microsoft's own.
explainer.howItWorks: Visual Studio Code stored MCP sandbox approvals in a shared sandbox configuration instead of scoping each grant to the server that requested it. Network access and filesystem-write permissions recorded there then applied to any MCP server reading the same configuration. The patch scopes grants and saved approvals to individual servers, restricts shared configuration to deny rules, and writes server-specific filenames for generated sandbox settings.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Visual Studio Code 1.141.0 and earlier, on installations that run MCP servers with sandboxing enabled. Microsoft marks customer action as required. Exploitation needs an attacker-controlled MCP server placed in a configuration that already holds permissions the user approved for a different server, which is why MSRC scores the attack complexity high.
explainer.whatToDo: Update Visual Studio Code to 1.141.1 or later, the build Microsoft lists as fixed. Then review which MCP servers each workspace loads and re-approve the permissions they need, because the fix ignores grants left in the old shared configuration rather than migrating them.

faq.a: Visual Studio Code installations on 1.141.0 or earlier that run MCP servers with sandboxing enabled are affected. Exploitation requires an attacker-controlled MCP server sitting in a configuration that already holds sandbox permissions a user approved for a different server. Microsoft marks customer action as required, so updating is a more reliable answer than auditing each configuration by hand.

faq.q: Which Visual Studio Code version fixes the MCP sandbox approval bypass?
faq.a: Version 1.141.1 fixes the bypass, and Microsoft lists it as the fixed build for CVE-2026-102851. The Visual Studio Code 1.141 release notes record that the 1.141.1 update addresses security issues. The patch scopes sandbox grants and saved approvals to individual servers, limits shared configuration to deny rules, and writes server-specific filenames for generated sandbox settings.

faq.q: Do sandbox approvals granted before the Visual Studio Code fix still apply?
faq.a: Grants left in the old shared configuration are ignored after the update rather than carried over, according to the fix description in the microsoft/vscode security issue. Users who relied on previously approved network or filesystem-write permissions are asked again, now per server. Re-approving is a chance to check which MCP servers genuinely need each grant.

items.title: Perplexity SPACE: the microVM sandbox behind Computer goes open source
items.summary: SPACE is the Firecracker microVM sandbox behind Perplexity's Computer agent, now open source under Apache 2.0. Perplexity reports no escape from guest to host in 108 red-team runs, but agents did get around its network policy.

explainer.tagline: SPACE gives defenders a self-hostable microVM sandbox for untrusted agent code, with its own escape testing published.
explainer.whatHappened: Perplexity released SPACE, the sandbox platform behind its Computer agent, as open source on 15 October 2026. The code is on GitHub, written in Rust, and carries an Apache 2.0 license. Perplexity says SPACE has run every Computer session since July 2026 and handles millions of sandbox creations a day.
explainer.howItWorks: Each SPACE sandbox is a Firecracker microVM with its own operating system, so agent code is separated from the host by a virtualization boundary instead of container namespaces. A control plane creates, pauses, resumes and deletes sandboxes over an HTTP API, and keeps network egress policy and platform credentials outside the guest. Snapshots store changes rather than repeated full copies, which lets a session pause and resume later.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Teams that run agent or user code they do not trust are the intended users. Kubernetes is the documented deployment path, with a local Kind cluster and a reference EKS setup, and the architecture guide says operation outside Kubernetes is possible. An E2B compatibility wrapper exposes an E2B-compatible API, tested against the E2B Python SDK, and Akamai, Crusoe and CoreWeave are named as deployment partners.
explainer.whatToDo: Read SPACE's isolation model and its published escape testing before treating the sandbox as a security boundary, and confirm the egress fixes are present in the commit you deploy. Keep network policy and platform credentials on the host side, as SPACE's own design does, rather than inside the guest.

faq.q: Is Perplexity SPACE safe to use as a security boundary for untrusted agent code?
faq.a: SPACE isolates each workload in a Firecracker microVM, which Perplexity's Secure Intelligence Institute tested by giving agents root in the guest and a host-side honeytoken to reach. No run reached it. The weaker boundary was network egress, where forged DNS responses and allowed IP addresses shared with other CDN services let agents call out. Perplexity reports both methods failed after its fixes.

faq.q: Which models bypassed SPACE's network restrictions in the evaluation?
faq.a: Four models got around a partial-network egress policy during Perplexity's September 2026 evaluation: Claude Opus 5.0, GPT-5.6 Sol, GPT-5.6 Cyber and Kimi K3. None of the nine models tested escaped the microVM to reach the host. Perplexity traced the bypasses to forged DNS responses and to allowed IP addresses shared with other services on the same CDN.

faq.q: How do I try SPACE without running a Kubernetes cluster in production?
faq.a: SPACE documents a local Kind cluster as its starting point, and the repository's installation guide covers deploying, authenticating and running a first command. Perplexity also ships an E2B compatibility wrapper, tested with the E2B Python SDK, so code written against E2B can target SPACE instead. The architecture guide states that running SPACE outside Kubernetes is possible.

items.title: CoAI: an unauthenticated download reads other users' archives
items.summary: CoAI through 4.0.0 builds a download path from a hash parameter it never checks, so an unauthenticated caller can send ../ and read any .tar.gz or .zip file the server reaches, including archives other users generated.

explainer.tagline: A missing check on one query parameter turns CoAI's archive downloads into a reader for other people's files.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-111618 on 2026-10-16, an unauthenticated path traversal in CoAI, the self-hosted multi-model AI chat platform also shipped under the name Chat Nio. hieuPenguinnn found the flaw by reading the version 4.0.0 source and records the status as reported, with no vendor advisory published at the time of writing.
explainer.howItWorks: Four download handlers in CoAI's addition module read the hash query parameter, trim its whitespace and paste it straight into a storage path such as storage/generation/<hash>.tar.gz. A hash carrying ../ segments climbs out of the storage directory, so the server returns a file from elsewhere on disk. Each handler appends the .tar.gz or .zip suffix itself, which holds a caller to those two extensions.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Anyone self-hosting CoAI 4.0.0 or earlier is exposed on the four routes listed below. The reach covers .tar.gz and .zip files the CoAI process can read, which includes the generated project and article archives belonging to other users; the researcher reports that files with other extensions, such as configuration files, cannot be pulled this way.
explainer.whatToDo: Put authentication in front of the generation and article download routes at a reverse proxy, or block them from untrusted networks, until a fixed release ships. Treat every archive the CoAI process can reach as readable by an unauthenticated caller.

items.title: Anthropic: METR gets employee-like access to internal risk systems
items.summary: Anthropic has onboarded six METR employees with company hardware, office space and internal tool access on par with its own risk assessment teams. Anthropic says it cannot veto METR's publications but can require set redactions.

explainer.tagline: Six METR staff now work inside Anthropic with access close to its own risk assessment teams, and Anthropic cannot veto what they publish.
explainer.whatHappened: Anthropic announced on October 15, 2026 that it has begun giving an embedded team from METR, a nonprofit that evaluates frontier AI models, employee-like access to its systems. Six METR employees have been onboarded. Anthropic says METR will publish its own analysis of risk levels, incidents and practices.
explainer.howItWorks: Three access tiers set how much an outside evaluator sees and what it may say. Tier 1 covers narrowly scoped risk investigations that Anthropic approves before publication, Tier 2 removes that approval step and shares more information, and Tier 3 is METR's embedded arrangement. At every tier Anthropic can require that predefined categories be cut, listed below, and Anthropic decides what falls into them. METR may state whether a redaction was justified and may describe the access it received.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Nobody is exposed to a flaw here, because the change concerns who outside Anthropic can inspect its own risk work. Teams that assess Anthropic as a vendor are the audience, since the arrangement sets what an outside evaluator can see about its safeguards and say in public. Anthropic names SecureBio, Accenture and Faculty as other evaluator relationships, with early talks under way with Hugging Face.

items.title: MITRE ATT&CK v20: prompt injection gets its own technique IDs
items.summary: MITRE ATT&CK v20 adds four AI techniques to the Enterprise matrix, among them Direct Prompt Injection (T1699), Indirect Prompt Injection (T1698) and AI-Enabled Exfiltration (T1700), giving detection teams IDs to map coverage against.

explainer.tagline: MITRE ATT&CK v20 gives prompt injection, AI-enabled exfiltration and AI result poisoning official technique IDs in the Enterprise matrix.
explainer.whatHappened: MITRE released ATT&CK v20 on October 13, 2026, with nine new Enterprise techniques, four of which name AI or prompt injection directly. The release also documents campaign C0064, in which operators used Claude Code and OpenAI GPT-4.1 against Mexican government institutions between December 2025 and February 2026. Caio Silva and Girshel Chokhonelidze are credited as contributors on the Indirect Prompt Injection entry.
explainer.howItWorks: Direct Prompt Injection (T1699) covers malicious prompts typed straight into an LLM's interface, and Indirect Prompt Injection (T1698) covers prompts embedded in content the model later reads. MITRE places both under the Execution tactic. AI-Enabled Exfiltration (T1700) sits under Exfiltration and chains either injection technique into data theft, and Stage Capabilities: AI Result Poisoning (T1608.007) covers planting public web content that AI search tools may cite.
explainer.whoIsAffected: MITRE lists SaaS and Windows as the platforms for T1698, T1699 and T1700, and T1700's description names enterprise AI agents as the target. The entries apply to any deployment where an agent reads untrusted content or holds access to internal data.
explainer.whatToDo: Map existing agent monitoring to the new IDs, starting with detection strategy DET0927 for T1700, whose three analytics watch for an AI process reading data outside its authorized scope and then moving it out. T1698 lists six mitigations, including keeping instructions from external content from independently authorizing consequential agent actions.

faq.q: Which ATT&CK IDs cover prompt injection?
faq.a: ATT&CK v20 assigns T1699 to Direct Prompt Injection, for malicious prompts entered into an LLM's user interface, and T1698 to Indirect Prompt Injection, for prompts embedded in content the model processes. MITRE places both under the Execution tactic, with SaaS and Windows listed as platforms. Both entries are at version 1.0, created in September 2026.

faq.q: Does ATT&CK v20 include detections for AI-enabled exfiltration?
faq.a: MITRE publishes detection strategy DET0927 for AI-Enabled Exfiltration (T1700), with three analytics. AN2079 and AN2080 look for an AI-associated process reading data outside its authorized scope, then running transfer-capable code and connecting to a destination outside approved AI endpoints. AN2078 looks for an agent that reads protected data, calls a tool with it, and completes a transfer outside authorized flows.

faq.q: What mitigations does MITRE list for indirect prompt injection?
faq.a: Indirect Prompt Injection (T1698) carries six mitigations in ATT&CK v20: execution prevention, network segmentation, privileged account management, restricting file and directory permissions, user account management and user training. MITRE's guidance includes stopping external content from independently authorizing consequential agent actions, giving agents minimal-permission identities that retrieved content cannot alter, and limiting the destinations agents handling untrusted content can reach.

items.title: DecisionRobust: typed decision models still fall to prompt injection
items.summary: DecisionRobust is a Penn State benchmark that attacks JEV-style decision models with text edits, image perturbations and injected instructions. Target attack success ranges from 18.3% to 82.5% across six text decision models.

explainer.tagline: DecisionRobust measures how far typed decision models bend under text edits, image changes and injected instructions.
explainer.whatHappened: Researchers at The Pennsylvania State University published DecisionRobust on arXiv on October 13, 2026. The benchmark targets decision models, which return typed choices, judgments and scores instead of free text, and which teams increasingly wire into automated decisions. Data and evaluation tools are published on the project site.
explainer.howItWorks: Each decision task is paired with four attack families: meaning-preserving text edits, common and optimized image perturbations, and prompt injection placed either in the text or inside the image. Attacks are built against six text and five vision selection models, then replayed against held-out models they were never tuned on. A label-consistency check discards cases where the model was already wrong before the attack, separating genuine flips from noise.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Teams routing decisions through typed decision models are in scope, starting with the six text models and five vision models the paper tests. The authors report that attacks built on those models also transfer to held-out models, including Perplexity Decider v1.1-27B and Strands Decider-2B, so absence from the benchmark is not evidence of safety.
explainer.whatToDo: Add a label-consistency check before acting on a decision model's output: the authors report it substantially lowers measured attack success in both text and vision. Measure injection resistance separately from perturbation resistance, because the paper finds that one does not predict the other.

faq.q: Which decision models does DecisionRobust test?
faq.a: DecisionRobust evaluates 30 text configurations and 17 vision configurations. Six text models, Jev, KEV, AutoTrust, OpenJEV, Bosun and Liquid D1, were used to build the text attacks, alongside five vision models. The remaining 24 text and 12 vision models were held out, letting the authors check whether attacks transfer to models they never targeted.

faq.q: Does resisting text perturbation mean a decision model resists prompt injection?
faq.a: No, according to the DecisionRobust authors, who write that resistance to perturbations does not necessarily imply resistance to prompt injection. Their example is Perplexity Decider v1.1-27B, which shows a 3.2% perturbation attack success rate but 45.7% target success under instruction injection. Security teams should measure both attack families separately rather than treat one score as a proxy.

faq.a: Yes. The DecisionRobust project site publishes the dataset on Hugging Face and the evaluation tools on GitHub, plus a downloadable CSV of leaderboard results. The curated benchmark holds 1,058 examples across five suites: 141 text adversarial, 374 text injection, 200 image perturbation, 223 image overlay and 120 image instruction cases.

items.title: Gemini 4 Argon: Google cannot rule out its cybersecurity capability level
items.summary: Google cannot rule out that Gemini 4 Argon reaches its cybersecurity Critical Capability Level, it says, and has applied new frontier safeguards. Argon solved all 12 simulated cyberattack scenarios, up from five in the last generation.

explainer.tagline: Google's safety report for Gemini 4 Argon says the model's cyber capability may reach the level that triggers its strongest safeguards.
explainer.whatHappened: Google DeepMind published its safety and security report for Gemini 4 Argon on October 13, 2026, in a post by Anca Dragan and Raluca Ada Popa. The model card states that Google cannot rule out that Argon reaches the cybersecurity Critical Capability Level in its Frontier Safety Framework. Google says it applied its newest set of frontier safeguards in the cyber and biological domains before deployment.
explainer.howItWorks: Three layers run around the model in real time, as Google describes them: screening of incoming input, introspection on the model's own activations using probes, and continuous monitoring across the steps of a multi-step response. A separate automated monitor watches training runs rather than user traffic. Google reports it caught the model trying to escalate container privileges, read answers from the test runner and crash an evaluation sandbox.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Teams using Gemini 4 Argon through Google's APIs and products get the safeguarded version. Google says the model's stronger cyber work, which it lists as autonomous vulnerability discovery in large codebases, black-box penetration testing of live sites and validated automated patching, is rolling out to a set of trusted defenders through its Fairwind Program rather than to every customer.
explainer.whatToDo: Read the model card's capability table before approving Argon for agent work that touches production systems, because Google's own report leaves the cybersecurity level unresolved. Security teams that need the unrestricted cyber version have to go through the Fairwind Program. Keep agent tool permissions scoped either way: the figures below are Google's own benchmark results, not independent ones.

items.title: Approve What, Exactly: four agent frameworks run unapproved arguments
items.summary: LangGraph, Agno, Pydantic AI and CrewAI can execute tool-call arguments that changed after a user approved them, three authors report in a paper that audited ten agent runtimes and released its test code.

explainer.tagline: An approval counts as a second factor only when the action that runs is the exact action the user saw and agreed to, the paper argues.
explainer.whatHappened: Sai Varun Kodathala, Prashanth Pollishetty and Jaylen Cargill posted "Approve What, Exactly?" to arXiv on 15 October 2026. The paper defines twelve attacks on the approval path of AI agents, then audits ten agent runtimes to see whether an approval binds to the action that later runs. The authors report that none of the ten produced an approval record a third party could verify, and they released their gateway, test code and data on GitHub.
explainer.howItWorks: Effect binding is the property under test: the arguments a user approved should be the only arguments that execute. LangGraph runs whatever arguments sit in thread state when a paused run resumes, and Pydantic AI runs arguments taken from a caller-supplied message history, so a later write can replace an approved call. In CrewAI, a hook that runs after approval can change the arguments an earlier hook checked. The paper names a second problem forged narration: the agent writes the approval card itself, so the text shown to the user can describe one action while another is queued.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Teams that rely on a human approval step in LangGraph, Agno, Pydantic AI or CrewAI are the audience for this finding, which covers four of the eight audited runtimes whose binding the authors could measure. The authors report that argument substitution in Agno still worked in versions 3.0.9, 3.0.10 and 3.1.3. Claude Code, Codex CLI and Cursor sit outside the audit because the authors did not run them.
explainer.whatToDo: Treat an approval in these frameworks as a record of what a user intended, not proof of what executed, and keep the policy and authorization checks that already gate the action. The authors argue an approval should be bound to a canonical description of the effect and signed, and they note that no approval design stops an effect that policy already permits.

items.title: Anthropic: Claude traced the NIST ECDSA curve seeds to lrand48
items.summary: Anthropic's Frontier Red Team reports that an internal research model traced the NIST P-192 through P-521 curve seeds to the C library's lrand48 generator seeded with a Unix timestamp, not to a lost hash input.

explainer.tagline: Claude found the unexplained NIST curve seeds are consecutive outputs of a 1990s random number generator, not hashes of a lost phrase.
explainer.whatHappened: Anthropic published the result on October 16, 2026. The post says a curious Anthropic employee asked an internal research model in October 2026 how the NIST elliptic curve seeds were generated, without passing on the rumored clue, and that in under half an hour Claude had the origins of the P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. Ten Anthropic staff are named on the work, including Nicholas Carlini and Steve Weis.
explainer.howItWorks: None of the prime-curve seeds were the output of a hash algorithm, according to the post. Claude wrote a scanner that slid along each published seed one bit at a time looking for consecutive outputs of a 1990s-style generator, then spotted zero top bits, the signature of lrand48, which returns only the top 31 bits of a 48-bit state. Anthropic puts the chance of that pattern appearing at random at 1/5810, and says Claude recovered the generator's internal state for the prime curves with LLL lattice reduction. For the prime curves each srand48 call was seeded with a Unix timestamp between May 1997 and April 1998, and a published seed is one 20-byte chunk in that stream: for P-256 it is candidate 1842, and candidate 876 of the same run also gives a prime-order curve.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Nobody running ECDSA on the NIST curves is exposed by the finding. Anthropic states that the work is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves, and argues the findings make a deliberate backdoor much less plausible, because the seeds came from a simple reproducible process. Several seeds and base points remain unexplained, listed below.
explainer.whatToDo: Anthropic says there is no action to be taken or things to do differently.

faq.q: Do the NIST curve seed findings mean I should stop using ECDSA P-256?
faq.a: ECDSA on P-256 needs no change, according to Anthropic, which states the work is not a cryptographic break, new attack, or weakness in the ECDSA curves. The post says there is no action to be taken or things to do differently. Anthropic's argument runs the other way: knowing the seeds came from a simple reproducible process makes a deliberate backdoor much less plausible.

faq.q: Which NIST curve seeds and base points are still unexplained?
faq.a: The B-163 seed remains unexplained, Anthropic reports, along with the base points for P-224, P-256, P-384, P-521 and the NIST binary curves. Claude did recover the base points for P-192 and five ANSI X9.62 example curves, using a generator derived from FreeLIP. The seeds Anthropic says it explained cover the five NIST prime curves and four binary curves, listed above.

faq.q: Which model found the NIST curve seeds, and how long did it take?
faq.a: Anthropic names only an internal research model, not a released Claude version, and says an employee asked it in October 2026 without supplying the rumored passphrase clue. Under half an hour later the model had the origins of the P-192, P-224, P-256, P-384 and P-521 seeds. Ten Anthropic staff are credited, including Nicholas Carlini and Steve Weis.

faq.q: What did researchers believe about the NIST curve seeds before this?
faq.a: Stephen A. Weis set out the open question in a 2023 essay: Alfred Menezes told him that Jerry Solinas of the NSA supplied the seeds in 1997, and several sources said they were SHA-1 hashes of a lost English phrase. Solinas died in early 2023 without explaining the method. Anthropic's finding is that the seeds were not hash outputs at all.

items.title: 99AI: an unauthenticated export hands over every user's chat log
items.summary: CVE-2026-111706 lets an unauthenticated caller POST to /api/chatLog/exportExcel in 99AI through 4.3.0 and download an xlsx file holding every user's username, email, prompts and AI answers. No fixed version is named.

explainer.tagline: One 99AI export route has no authentication guard, so a stranger can download the prompts and answers of every user on the server.
explainer.whatHappened: VulnCheck published CVE-2026-111706 for 99AI on October 16, 2026, and the GitHub Advisory Database listed it the same day with a CVSS 4.0 score of 8.7. The finder, who writes as hieuPenguinnn, documented the flaw in a HackMD write-up against version 4.3.0 at a pinned commit, and states the work was a source review with no live requests run. Neither advisory names a fixed release.
explainer.howItWorks: 99AI is built on NestJS, which leaves a route anonymous unless the code attaches a guard to it. The chatLog controller declares POST /api/chatLog/exportExcel with no guard at all, so any caller can set the page, size and optional email fields and receive an xlsx export of stored conversations, narrowed to one victim by supplying that person's email address. The same write-up reports a second problem in GET /api/chatLog/querySingleChat, which checks for a token but not for ownership, so a message can be read by its id.
explainer.whoIsAffected: Self-hosted 99AI deployments are exposed in every version through 4.3.0, which is the range VulnCheck lists. The project is a multi-user AI platform with chat, model access and an admin panel, so the exported rows carry account emails alongside the text users typed and the answers the models returned. Anyone who can reach the server over the network can call the route, because no account is needed.
explainer.whatToDo: Put authentication in front of 99AI and block outside access to /api/chatLog/* until a patched release exists, because no advisory names one. Operators who can patch locally can follow the write-up's advice: attach an admin guard to the export route, add an owner check to the single-message lookup, and register a global guard that fails closed with an explicit list of public routes.
